stories.headline: Manchester City charges: Features, explainers, what's next after guilty verdict
stories.summary: ESPN has you covered with everything you need to know about the latest in the Manchester City scandal.
stories.body:
After an investigation spanning years, Manchester City were found guilty on more than 100 charges of serious breaches of Premier League financial regulations. The decision is a major development in one of the biggest scandals in soccer history, but the saga is far from over.

What happens next? What does the ruling mean for England's dominant force over the past decade, its fans and its players? ESPN's writers have you covered on every angle, from transfer implications to the mood at City's rival clubs.

Check back here for the latest as this story continues to unfold.

Tighe: Man City's alternate universe: Guardiola, Haaland to Arsenal? Arteta to PSG?
What would the sport have looked like if City had not spent in the way that they did? Who would have won the eight league titles? Where would the superstars (like Erling Haaland) they signed have gone instead? And what would manager Pep Guardiola's career have looked like without a decade-long stint in Manchester?

Lindop: Was epic Man City-Liverpool rivalry all a sham after cheating scandal?
Under Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola, Liverpool and Man City pushed the Premier League's standards higher than ever. But was it all a sham?

Dawson: 'We're Not Really Here': As Man City sanctions loom, it's the fans who suffer
Manchester City's financial malfeasance could send the club back down the football pyramid, a place where fans of a certain age are very familiar.

Olley: Arsenal fight back to win as Premier League resumes under cloud of Man City verdict
Does Arsenal's comeback win over Leeds close the gap on leaders Man City, or extend their own lead at the top? This is the perpetual uncertainty that hangs over the Premier League now.

Ogden: What's next for Man City? Appeals, possible punishments, how long it could take
Man City have appealed the Premier League's guilty verdict, while the sanctions board also begins its work on figuring out appropriate punishments. So what happens next, and what is the possible timeline?

Marcotti: We don't get Man City guilty verdict without hacker Rui Pinto, but it doesn't make him a hero
It's worth reminding ourselves that the Manchester City case, which has rocked English football to its foundation, would never have seen the light of day without a spiky-haired college dropout turned self-taught hacker named Rui Pinto.

O'Hanlon: Mock draft: How would Premier League teams pick if Man City cheating scandal took a turn?
Now that Manchester City have been found to have cheated on a huge scale, anything is on the table -- maybe even an American-style Premier League draft?

Multiple contributors: How top Premier League clubs view Man City's guilty verdict
Four clubs (Arsenal, Liverpool, Man United and Tottenham) retained their legal rights in the Premier League's case against Man City. Now that a guilty verdict has been issued, what will they do in response?

Ogden: How a mass Man City player exodus would warp the transfer market
If Manchester City are punished by being relegated from the Premier League, group of players worth more than £1 billion in transfer fees would suddenly become available.

Dawson: How Man City players, staff are handling Premier League verdict
As the reaction to Man City's guilty verdict continues to ripple across the sporting world, the club's internal messaging is very much one of confidence and carrying on. That might be easier said than done.

Olley: Manchester City guilty charges explained: Premier League's options, how appeal works
Man City's guilty verdict is a landmark moment. But what comes next? What punishments are on the table, and how does the appeals process work?

Ogden: Does Man City's guilty verdict impact Guardiola's legacy as an all-time coaching great?
Pep Guardiola won 16 major honors as Man City manager. They all now count for nothing after the Premier League found the club guilty of systematically breaking financial rules.

Marcotti: Hard to see how Man City recover from extraordinary guilty verdict
The confirmation that Manchester City were found guilty by the Premier League on over 100 breaches of financial regulations has sent shock waves through the sport. How do Man City survive this?

Dawson: Man City's guilt the talk of the town around English soccer
Man City being found guilty of 100-plus charges by the Premier League was the only topic of conversation around Manchester, and lower-league games, in the first weekend of action since the verdict.

Ogden: Man City verdict will leave a stain and stench on a Premier League era
Manchester City have been found guilty of almost all 115 financial charges against them. It means an era of English soccer is now tarnished with multiple asterisks.

stories.headline: 2026 WNBA Finals feature record African representation as Golden State, Atlanta chase first title
stories.summary: For the first time in WNBA history, the Finals will feature three players and one executive with African connections, the highest African representation in the championship series dating to the league's inaugural season in 1997.
stories.body:
History will be made when the 2026 WNBA Finals between the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream tips off this Saturday.

For the first time in league history, the Finals will feature three players and one executive with African connections, the highest African representation in the championship series dating to the league's inaugural season in 1997.

Ghanaian-American general manager Ohemaa Nyanin and Canadian forward Laeticia Amihere, whose parents are Ghanaian, represent Golden State, while on the other side, Atlanta have Mali international Sika Kone and Kenyan center Madina Okot.

The four surpass the previous high of three from 2008, when players Olayinka Sanni (Detroit Shock) and Morenike Atunrase (San Antonio Silver Stars) were on opposing teams, with Mike Ekanem serving as strength and conditioning coach for San Antonio.

All three are of Nigerian heritage, and Sanni even represented Nigeria, winning two silver medals and one bronze across three All Africa Games tournaments.

This year's Finals, which begin Saturday in San Francisco, brings together two franchises seeking their first WNBA championship, with Nyanin's leadership of Golden State's basketball operations introducing an executive dimension to Africa's history in the league.

Appointed the Valkyries' inaugural general manager in May 2024, Nyanin became the first executive of African origin in the WNBA, and has overseen one of the fastest rises by an expansion franchise in WNBA history.

Under her leadership, Golden State became the first WNBA expansion team to qualify for the playoffs in their inaugural season in 2025 and followed that by reaching the Finals in only their second season, another expansion franchise record.

The Valkyries finished the 2026 regular season 32-12 before advancing through the playoffs, including a semifinal victory over defending champion Las Vegas Aces.

Nyanin, who previously served as assistant general manager of the New York Liberty team that reached the 2023 Finals, finished third in voting for the WNBA's 2026 Executive of the Year award.

Golden State's success has also been accompanied by record commercial growth. The franchise became the first professional women's sports team to surpass $100 million in annual revenue and topped the WNBA's franchise valuation rankings at about $1 billion, according to May 2026 estimates by CNBC.

The Valkyries also sold out all 44 regular-season home games across their first two seasons, extending their sellout streak through the playoffs.

Although the commercial achievements fall under the wider franchise leadership, Nyanin has been responsible for constructing the roster that has taken Golden State to the championship series in only their second year, a remarkable accomplishment.

Amihere, who was born in Canada to Ghanaian parents, is one member of that roster. The 6-foot-4 forward won the NCAA championship with South Carolina in 2022, helping coach Dawn Staley's Gamecocks defeat Connecticut in the title game. She made history as a teenager in 2017 when, at 15, she became the first Canadian woman to dunk in a competitive game.

The forward was selected eighth overall by Atlanta Dream in the 2023 WNBA draft and has represented Canada at the Olympic Games, including Tokyo in 2021 and Paris in 2024. Her move to Golden State has now brought her to the WNBA Finals for the first time, adding another milestone to a career that has included college and international basketball success.

On the other side of the floor, Atlanta's African representation comes through two players who have followed different routes to the WNBA.

Kone is an established Mali international who developed through one of Africa's most successful women's basketball programs. She was named MVP of the 2021 FIBA Under-19 Women's Basketball World Cup, after leading Mali to a fourth-place finish, the best result by an African team in the tournament's history.

The now 24-year-old averaged 19.7 points and 14.8 rebounds during that competition and was subsequently selected by New York Liberty with the 29th overall pick in the 2022 WNBA draft.

She has also represented Mali at senior level, including at the Women's AfroBasket, where the country has remained one of the leading challengers to Nigeria's continental dominance.

Her appearance on Atlanta's Finals roster continues Mali's history in the championship series. Hamchetou Maiga-Ba won the championship with Sacramento Monarchs in 2005 and returned to the Finals the following year, when Sacramento lost to Detroit Shock.

Okot, meanwhile, has emerged as Kenya's most prominent women's basketball export. The 6-foot-6 center began playing basketball at 16 after initially pursuing volleyball in Kenya, before moving to the United States and establishing herself in college basketball.

She averaged 11.3 points and 9.6 rebounds at Mississippi State during the 2024-25 season before transferring to South Carolina, where she helped the Gamecocks reach the NCAA championship game in 2026. Okot averaged 12.8 points and 10.6 rebounds in her final college season, recording 22 double-doubles.

Atlanta selected her with the 13th overall pick in the 2026 WNBA draft, making her the first Kenyan player selected in the first round, and only the third in league history, following Josephine Owino, a third-round selection in 2009, and Kenyan-American Olivia Nelson-Ododa, who was drafted in the second round in 2022.

Such is the huge influence that Okot has become in Kenya, that the country's President William Ruto came to watch her play in Atlanta's 83-65 victory over New York Liberty in September.

Ruto, who was in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, attended the game with First Lady Rachel Ruto, NBA Deputy Commissioner Mark Tatum and representatives of NBA Africa. Afterward, Ruto and his wife met Okot on the court, took photographs and spoke with her in Swahili.

In her rookie season, she averaged 5.4 points and 3.3 rebounds in 42 regular-season appearances as the Dream returned to the Finals for the first time since 2013.

The presence of the four African-connected figures continues a history dating to the early years of the WNBA. In 2001, just four years after the first Finals, DR Congo's Mwadi Mabika helped the Los Angeles Sparks defeat Charlotte Sting, whose roster included another African, Mozambique's Clarisse Machanguana. Both became the first players of African origin to appear in the Finals.

Mabika returned to the Finals to win a second championship with Los Angeles in 2002, this time against New York Liberty and fellow Congolese player Bernadette Ngoyisa Mudju. But a year later, she was on the other side, as Senegal's Astou Ndiaye-Diatta won the championship with Detroit Shock, defeating Mabika and the Sparks.

Those three consecutive Finals established an early precedent for African-born players appearing on opposing teams in the championship series. In total, players of African origin have been in 15 of the league's 29 previous Finals, with 16 distinct players and 22 total player appearances.

Nigeria, as expected, have had more players in WNBA Finals roster than any other African country, with five including Sanni, Natalia Achonwa, Ogwumike, Liz Cambage and Ezi Magbegor.

Los Angeles have also won more championships with African-connected players than any other franchise, claiming three through Mabika's two titles and Nigerian-American forward Ogwumike's championship in 2016.

Ogwumike, who won the league's MVP award that season, scored the decisive basket in Game 5 against Minnesota Lynx and returned to the Finals in 2017, but was second time unlucky when Los Angeles lost the title to Minnesota.

Mabika remains the most successful African-born player in league history, with two titles from three Finals appearances. Eight players of African origin have been WNBA champions, for a total of nine titles.

These include Seattle Storm's Magbegor, whose family has Nigerian roots, in 2020; Senegal-born Astou Ndour-Fall with Chicago Sky in 2021; and Nyara Sabally, whose father is Gambian, with New York Liberty in 2024, along with Hamchetou Maiga-Ba, and Olayinka Sanni.

The African connection also extended beyond the playing roster. Ekanem's involvement with San Antonio in 2008 helped establish the previous high for African representation in a Finals series, while Nigerian origin athletic trainer Michelle Anumba was part of the Las Vegas Aces' back-to-back championship teams in 2022 and 2023.

This year's championship series adds the front office into that history, with Nyanin overseeing the basketball operations of a Golden State team attempting to win a title in only their second season.

Atlanta, who have lost three previous Finals appearances in 2010, 2011 and 2013, are hoping to heal from the trauma of those losses by putting the memory behind them to claim their first championship in franchise history.

The series opens on Saturday at Chase Center, with one franchise guaranteed to win its first WNBA title. But more importantly for Africa, whichever team wins that first chip, there will be at least two Africans on the podium when that final buzzer goes.

stories.headline: Brewers sweep the Dodgers in the NLCS to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982
stories.summary: — Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer off reliever Tanner Scott in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series...
stories.body:
LOS ANGELES -- — Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer off reliever Tanner Scott in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to earn their first trip to the World Series since 1982.


No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off reliever Edwin Díaz gave the Brewers a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.


Shohei Ohtani's first home run of the postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 early before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending World Series champions a year after getting swept by the Dodgers in the NLCS.


The Brewers lost to the St. Louis Cardinals 4-3 in their only other World Series appearance, when Milwaukee played in the American League.

stories.headline: USMNT players are beefing online again: A look at the most memorable, pettiest feuds
stories.summary: A new argument between USMNT players has caused a stir, continuing a long tradition of American stars beefing for no reason.
stories.body:
Death, taxes, and current/former U.S. men's national team players publicly starting quarrels.

It seems as though the American soccer scene can't go through long stretches without a high-profile figure starting a beef, and on Thursday, retired striker Eddie Johnson caused a stir after calling out national team legend Landon Donovan.

"You talk so much s--- about every other young upcoming player in the past but yourself lol why don't we talk about the 5 years you were in Germany and failed and ran back to MLS bc you weren't good enough? Why don't we speak about this?" Johnson wrote on social media, with a screenshot to a quote from Donovan, who discussed the growing excitement over up-and-coming star Cavan Sullivan.

Donovan pointed out former prodigy Freddy Adu, as well as Johnson, as part of his argument to calm expectations.

"One of the best considerably players in our country failed in Europe early in his career," Johnson continued. "No one killed him but he's killing all these young players that have done more then he ever has done in Europe."

This kind of spicy-but-ridiculous online drama is nothing new for the USMNT.

The lore of public and unnecessary beefs involving the USMNT is like a tradition. In an attempt to highlight some of the previous chapters -- sticking to the silliest and most pointless beefs rather than the more serious ones -- we've made a short list of some memorable incidents.

Landon Donovan vs. Christian Pulisic: 'It's pissing me off'

This isn't the first time Donovan appears on this list -- and it won't be the last, either.

After star player Christian Pulisic asked to take the summer off during the 2025 Gold Cup, Donovan called out USMNT players who missed the tournament.

"This is what it means to represent your country," Donovan said of Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo while working as a pundit during the UEFA Nations League final.

"Forty years old. He's played a long-ass season. He's tired. He's out there grinding. Hurt himself in the process, and I can't help but think about some of our guys on vacation, not wanting to play in the Gold Cup. It's pissing me off."

Pulisic's father responded on social media by posting ChatGPT's explanation for Donovan's 144-day sabbatical in 2012-13 that later saw him left out of the 2014 World Cup squad.

"Landon Donovan took his sabbatical because he was feeling both physically and mentally exhausted after years of intense competition and the pressure that comes with being a top athlete," read a screenshot that included the AI text.

Pulisic hit "like" on the post.

Jermaine Jones vs. Jordan Morris: 'Really? Why you go the easy way?'

Justifiably flustered after the USMNT's failure to qualify for the 2018 World Cup, midfielder Jermaine Jones, who had recently been left off the national team roster, shared his complaints about the U.S. team on Instagram Live.

While criticizing players who never take a chance abroad in Europe, Jones specifically put a spotlight on Seattle Sounders forward Jordan Morris, saying that Morris turned down an opportunity to play in Germany.

According to Jones, Morris told him: "I want to go home. My dad is a doctor in Seattle, and my mom, they bought me and my girlfriend a dog."

"Really?" said Jones during the livestream. "Why you go the easy way when you have the chance?"

Morris has since said that the dog was not a factor, saying: "I obviously didn't stay in Seattle because of a dog."

Alejandro Bedoya vs. Jozy Altidore: 'You have a lot to say but never to anyone's face'

After USMNT teammates Alejandro Bedoya and Jozy Altidore faced off in an MLS match in 2017, Bedoya was asked postgame whether a penalty decision for Altidore was correct.

"Knowing him, he tends to go down easily in the box," Bedoya said just weeks before a national team camp. "So, just leave it at that."

That didn't sit well with Altidore, who took to social media.

"Nice comment pal," he wrote. "You have a lot to say but never to anyones face. Im surprised.. but I shouldn't be."

Both later downplayed the back-and-forth, but it was still clear that Bedoya had struck a nerve.

Eric Wynalda vs. Landon Donovan: 'There's a big part of me that wants to stuff a sock in your mouth right now'

Last year, Donovan gained attention after he said that rising star Diego Luna should remain in MLS, and not move to Europe just yet, to cement a place for the USMNT's 2026 World Cup roster.

It was an eyebrow-raising comment, which provoked former striker Eric Wynalda to rant about Donovan's advice during his "Unleashed with Eric Wynalda" show.

"Stop polluting minds because it's getting f---ing annoying. Nobody believes that, Landon," Wynalda said. "Nobody even comes close to believing that this place is the best place to get ready for a World Cup.

"I don't want to get into these fights, but there's a big part of me that wants to stuff a sock in your mouth right now. It's getting annoying as hell."

Wynalda has previously noted that he has "never been friends" with Donovan. Big surprise!

Tim Weah vs. former USMNT players: 'I just feel like they're really evil'

Let's go back to when Pulisic took a break during the 2025 Gold Cup.

It occurred during the filming of the "Pulisic" documentary, which highlighted the criticism that the current national team was receiving from former national team players about the squad's performances and the commitment of someone like Pulisic.

"I think those guys are chasing checks and, for me, I just feel like they're really evil," Pulisic's teammate Tim Weah said in the documentary. "They've been players, and they know what it's like when you're getting bashed. Those are the same guys that'll turn around and shake your hand and try to be friendly with you at the end of the day."

Weah later stood by his comments after being asked whether he regretted them.

stories.headline: Defense bails out Broncos in OT win as Nix, offense struggle
stories.summary: The Broncos' D came up with five sacks, 17 QB hits and two interceptions, enabling Denver to win even though the offense finished with only 168 net yards.
stories.body:
DENVER -- With a 17-14 overtime win over the Seattle Seahawks finally in hand, Denver Broncos linebacker Nik Bonitto was still trying to wrap his head around one of the numbers that told the story of the night.

The Broncos (4-2) had survived, somehow, despite the fact that the team's defense faced 82 snaps Thursday night in Empower Field at Mile High, just four days after a road win at the Los Angeles Chargers.

"82 snaps? Did I feel 82 snaps? Bro, every one of them," Bonitto said with a tired smile.

The Broncos' defense sacked Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold five times, hit him 17 times and intercepted him twice, including once in overtime to set up Wil Lutz's 53-yard winning field goal with 4 minutes, 53 seconds left. It all enabled the Broncos to win even though Denver's offense finished with only 168 net yards and didn't have a drive longer than five plays on its last nine possessions of regulation.

The Broncos, without injured Pat Surtain II and Talanoa Hufanga, still had 12 different players hit Darnold at least once, believed by the team to be the most in an NFL game since at least 2006. It also was the second time this season the Broncos' defense had faced 82 plays (the Week 3 win over the Los Angeles Rams was the other) but this time it was on a short week.

"Defensively we were magnificent,'' Broncos coach Sean Payton said. "I don't know how many times we hit the quarterback, we got three takeaways. ... The takeaways were huge ... that was the difference, field position, all of that. They were fantastic.''

Said Broncos linebacker Justin Strnad: "We pride ourselves on being a dominant unit and we felt like we were that tonight. We knew we were going to get after [Darnold], that was part of the plan and we did that.''

The night didn't have that kind of start. The Broncos' offense put together two long scoring drives in their first three possessions, a season-most 16-play, 74-yard touchdown drive, followed by a nine-play, 79-yard touchdown drive that gave Denver a 14-3 lead.

But in the nine Denver possessions between the second touchdown and Lutz's overtime kick, the offense punted seven times, had a drive go for minus-5 yards to end the half and ended regulation with a possession for a 1-yard loss. The Broncos didn't run more than five plays on any of those possessions, and that put the defense back on the field over and over again without much recovery time.

"We don't win that game without them,'' Broncos quarterback Bo Nix said of the defense.

"We kind of knew it was going to be that kind of game; obviously we want the offense to get rolling a little bit and figure that out,'' Strnad said. "But we're going to do absolutely anything we can to keep winning week in, week out.''

The Broncos had only one game all of last season in which the defense played more than 80 snaps -- 85 against the Washington Commanders last Nov. 30 -- and had only two games in all of 2024 in which the defense played more than 75 snaps.

Thursday's performance left the Broncos, who faced five playoff teams from 2025 and both teams from the NFC Championship Game over the season's first six weeks, at 4-2 despite their offensive miscues. Nix's 107 yards passing in Thursday's win was the second-lowest total in a game of his career, and two of his three lowest single-game totals have now come in the span of four days, as he had 123 yards passing against the Los Angeles Chargers.

The Broncos' longest play of the game was 16 yards.

"We're definitely capable [of better]; I don't know where the disconnect is right now to be honest with you,'' Nix said. "I just think we're really struggling to find those explosive plays and that's what makes an offensive spectacular is explosive plays and right now we don't have those.''

The Seahawks scored 11 fourth-quarter points as the Broncos' defense began to show signs of fatigue, including on an 11-play, 67-yard touchdown drive. Seattle also opened overtime with the ball and had a third-and-7 from the Broncos' 28-yard line when Ja'Quan McMillian snatched a pass intended for Seahawks wide receiver Rashid Shaheed.

Four plays later, Lutz kicked the winner.

"It was a real challenge for us and I like the way we handled it,'' Bonitto said.

stories.headline: F1 2027 driver lineups: Who has a seat - and who's out of contract?
stories.summary: The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.
stories.body:
The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.

Most drivers secured short-term deals to survive the regulation shift, leaving the grid wide open for the following year. With only a handful of drivers locked into long-term contracts almost every seat on the grid is up for grabs.

Here is our early look at what the future holds for the current Formula 1 lineup.

McLaren

Lando Norris - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2030

Prior to the start of the 2024 F1 season Norris agreed to an "extended multi-year contract beyond 2025."

The reigning champion has now signed a new contract with McLaren until at least 2030. The deal, which includes one of his title-winning Formula 1 cars as a gift from the team, also has the option of a "multi-year" extension beyond 2030.

Oscar Piastri - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Ahead of the first race of the 2025 F1 season Piastri also signed a multi-year contract extension. His previous deal already ran until the end of 2026, and his latest agreement is likely to keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2028 -- though speculation continues to rumble on about his long-term future.

Ferrari

Lewis Hamilton - 2027

While an exact end date of Hamilton's contract -- signed after completing one of the biggest driver moves in F1 history -- was never officially communicated, Hamilton admitted earlier this year that he still had a contract in place for 2027. That means he got at least a three-year deal at Ferrari, something he had also been seeking at Mercedes.

Amid retirement rumours, Hamilton has also crushed speculation and assured fans that he wasn't going anywhere just yet.

He said: "There's a lot of people that are trying to retire me, and that's not even in my thoughts. I'm already thinking of what will be next, and planning for, like, the next five years. But I still plan to be here for some time."

Charles Leclerc - 2028

Leclerc, who first joined Ferrari in 2019, signed another multi-year extension ahead of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

The team did not publicly reveal an exact expiry date, but the new agreement is understood to take Leclerc to 2028 and potentially beyond, giving Ferrari long-term security over one side of its driver lineup.

Red Bull

Max Verstappen - 2030

Red Bull confirmed in 2022 that four-time world champion Verstappen would remain with the team until the end of 2028 in one of the longest deals on the F1 grid.

Sources told ESPN that performance-related clauses in Verstappen's contract could allow him to leave early, but the Dutchman has now signed a new contract extension with Red Bull until 2030 ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix.

Isack Hadjar - 2027

Isack Hadjar was promoted from Racing Bulls to partner Verstappen for the 2026 season after an impressive rookie campaign. He has now signed a contract extension with Red Bull, securing his seat for the 2027 season.

Mercedes

George Russell - beyond 2026

Russell agreed a new deal with Mercedes ahead of the 2026 season following lengthy negotiations with team principal Toto Wolff.

Although the agreement was initially confirmed as taking him through at least 2026, Russell has since described it as a multi-year deal and said he will fulfill the performance clauses in his contract to stay at Mercedes next year.

Kimi Antonelli - TBC

Mercedes' Antonelli has only been given one-year contracts since his debut, but given his form this season there's no way he'll be leaving the Silver Arrows. Right?

No official announcements have been made yet, but Antonelli could be celebrating both a maiden title and a bumper new deal this year.

Aston Martin

Fernando Alonso - TBC

Alonso's current Aston Martin deal runs until the end of the 2026 season, and he said a decision on his future will come later in the year. At 45 years old, the decision is likely to be between continuing with an underperforming Aston Martin team, or calling time on his F1 career once and for all.

Lance Stroll - TBC

Stroll signed a contract extension in 2024 which kept him with Aston Martin for 2025 "and beyond," but no specific end date was announced. Part of that ambiguity, of course, is because he's the son of team owner Lawrence Stroll.

He remains with the team for 2026, although his position for 2027 has not formally been confirmed.

Alpine

Pierre Gasly - 2028

Gasly is one of the drivers whose future is already settled -- the Frenchman signed a new multi-year agreement with Alpine in 2025 which keeps him locked in at the team until at least the end of the 2028 season.

Franco Colapinto - 2027

Colapinto retained his Alpine seat alongside Gasly for 2026 after taking over from Jack Doohan during the previous season. He has now signed a new contract with the team, meaning the Argentinian will continue with Alpine for the 2027 season.

Haas

Rafael Câmara - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2027

F2 star Câmara will replace Esteban Ocon for the 2027 season on a multi-year agreement. The reigning Formula 3 champion and current Formula 2 leader will make his debut in F1 and will partner fellow Ferrari Driver Academy member Oliver Bearman.

Oliver Bearman - TBC

Bearman joined Haas on a multi-year deal when he became a full-time F1 driver in 2025. The exact duration of Bearman's contract has not been made public, leaving his 2027 status uncertain for now.

However, sources with good knowledge of the team's thinking have told ESPN that Bearman is almost certain to stay with the team in 2027 unless a Ferrari seat opens up, then the Englishman remains effectively loaned to Haas.

Racing Bulls

Liam Lawson - TBC

Lawson remained with Racing Bulls for 2026 after rebuilding his season following a short-lived promotion to Red Bull the previous year.

His seat is only confirmed for the current season, meaning the New Zealander will again have to prove his case if he is to stay within the Red Bull set-up in 2027.

Arvid Lindblad - TBC

Lindblad became the latest Red Bull junior to make the jump to Formula 1 when he was handed a Racing Bulls seat for 2026.

The rookie is currently only confirmed for this season and the team have played down speculation over their driver lineup for 2027. You'd be shocked to see him go anywhere, though.

Williams

Carlos Sainz - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Sainz originally joined Williams on a deal covering the 2025 and 2026 seasons, with "options to extend" his stay beyond that. He has recently spoken about wanting to make the Williams project work, leading to him signing a new multi-year extension with the team.

Alex Albon - 2027

Albon signed a new one-year contract with Williams during the summer break, tying him down for the 2027 season. The short-term deal is interesting, given Albon's last contract -- signed in 2024 -- was for multiple years. Keeping those options open?

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg - TBC

Hulkenberg joined Sauber ahead of its transformation into the Audi team on a multi-year contract in 2025.

There are believed to be options in his deal which could allow him to remain with Audi beyond 2026, but an exact end date has not been announced.

Gabriel Bortoleto - TBC

Bortoleto joined Hulkenberg at Sauber before the team's transition to Audi and also signed a multi-year deal.

The Brazilian is contracted through at least the end of 2026, but his place for 2027 has not yet been officially confirmed.

Cadillac

Sergio Perez - 2027

Perez returned to the Formula 1 grid with Cadillac for the team's debut season in 2026 after spending a year away from racing.

The Mexican joined on a multi-year agreement understood to be on similar terms to teammate Valtteri Bottas, putting him in line to remain with Cadillac for 2027.

Valtteri Bottas - 2027

Bottas also returned to a full-time race seat with Cadillac after spending 2025 as Mercedes' reserve driver.

The Finn signed a multi-year deal which runs until at least the end of 2027, giving the new team one of the few already settled driver pairings heading into next season.

stories.headline: Shakhtar's Champions League win vs. AEK was more than just a game
stories.summary: Shakhtar Donetsk haven't played at home since 2014 due to the war, and this season, their Champions League home games are at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge. Wednesday's win was a reminder of how absurd their situation is.
stories.body:
LONDON -- Take a step back and revel in the absurdity for a minute. Shakhtar Donetsk, a Ukrainian team from the Russian-speaking part of the country, are playing a Greek team, AEK Athens, in London, at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge. Technically, it's a "home game," but that concept has become rather meaningless.

Shakhtar haven't played at their home, the Donbas Arena, since May 2014, some 650 weeks ago. They turn up wherever someone will host them: Odessa, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Lviv for Ukrainian league games; Warsaw, Hamburg, Gelsenkirchen, Krakow, Ljubljana and now London for matches in European competition. Why? Because their opponents can't (or won't) travel to Ukraine, where none of the civilian airports are open, air raid sirens go off a dozen times a day, and where drones and bombs can't be trusted to distinguish between a military captain and the captain of a soccer team.

It's pretty obvious that in those circumstances, you're more than a club -- you're a symbol of defiance, an attempt to maintain some sort of normality in the face of a war that has taken more than half a million lives and displaced tens of millions more.

"We are playing for people from Ukraine all over the world," sporting director Dario Srna said. "Everywhere we've gone, they've come [to see us]. We represent Ukraine in the center of the world: we're not just playing for us. [We are] a Ukrainian team, we are not just Shakhtar."

But, of course, nothing is normal. Everything is messed up, and their mere presence in the Champions League constitutes a political dimension.

Wednesday night, Shakhtar were at Stamford Bridge, the home of Chelsea. Resourceful as ever, street vendors outside the ground hawked their off-brand scarves, except rather than "Cole Palmer," "João Pedro" and "John Terry," the names read "Pedrinho," "[Mykola] Matviyenko" and "[Valeriy] Bondar." Watching over them was a life-size cardboard cutout of Dwayne Johnson, aka The Rock, only his face was replaced by that of Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelenskyy.

Inside, visiting AEK fans -- who turned the Shed End into a two-tier wall of tifo, flags and noise -- outsing, if not outnumber, the "home" support.

Because yes, this is Shakhtar's home for the Champions League this season, a move made possible by the London club's failure to qualify for European competitions (and, probably, a need to rake in some extra rent on those empty weeknights). Ironically, Chelsea's previous owner, Roman Abramovich, was forced by the U.K. government to sell the club after the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, because of his ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Abramovich holds passports from Portugal, Israel and Russia. His yachts are moored in Turkey.

Abramovich, whose mother is Ukrainian, is a complicated figure. So is Shakhtar's version of Abramovich, Rinat Akhmetov.

An ethnic Russian, but Donetsk-born and bred, Akhmetov's huge wealth from mining and energy bankrolled the club's rise to prominence prewar -- lest we forget, the likes of Willian and Fernandinho, Henrikh Mkiytaryan and Douglas Costa are all Shakhtar alums -- and keeps it alive and very much kicking today. Forbes estimates his wealth at nearly $8 billion and like most folks of that ilk, Akhmetov could easily have made different choices, decamping abroad. When the war broke out, he chose to stay, and that was not something to take for granted, given that he had previously clashed with Zelenskyy and, in the 2000s, served in parliament in the party of former pro-Russian Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych, whom he also backed financially.

Akhmetov broke with Yanukovych in 2014 and while his pro-Ukrainian words today are loud, his actions -- from staying in the country to tirelessly campaigning to his efforts with Shakhtar -- speak even louder.

"He can't leave Ukraine, not after seeing what he has seen," Srna says of Akhmetov. "It's impossible. He's devoted himself to this, helping the economy, helping the people. All while sleeping each night under bombs."

Many Ukrainians have no choice, which makes the actions of those who could be elsewhere all the more remarkable. It takes an unconventional type of person.

Most of Shakhtar's players are Brazilian -- lured by money, sure, but also the opportunity to showcase their talent. The coach, former Atletico Madrid and Barcelona standout Arda Turan, is Turkish. Even if you don't remember what he was like as a player, watching him prowl the technical area during the AEK game, fists clenched and eyes wild, you come to understand how this is the same guy who once got into an altercation with a pop star in an Istanbul hospital, a brawl that ended in him firing a gun into the floor.

Srna himself is Croatian, but has been at the club -- first as a player then as sporting director -- for 23 years. He too could have left umpteen times and, in fact, he says he even turned down the chance to take over Barcelona's recruitment a decade ago.

"Ukraine and Shakhtar are in my blood," he says. "If I leave now, I couldn't live with myself."

In some ways, Srna has been here before. He was eight years old when civil war broke out in the former Yugoslavia in March 1991. The conflict that would rage for 4½ years, ripped apart communities along ethnic lines. Neighbors took up arms against neighbors. His own father woke up every day supplying baked goods for the military. If you've seen the ESPN 30 for 30 documentary "Once Brothers" about the relationship between Drazen Petrovic and Vlade Divac, well ... he lived it. Twice. Maybe that's why he soldiers on, numb to what he is experiencing.

"I have this feeling inside myself," he says. "It's a feeling I felt before [as a child experiencing war in Croatia]. But when you feel that pain and it comes back to you again, well, you're not going to have the same pain twice. I know this pain. I know this feeling ..."

Srna trails off as he searches for the right words of history -- the worst parts -- repeating itself with him in the middle of it. But then he flickers back with righteous anger.

"This is unbelievable, I can't explain it," he says. "Four-and-a-half years [this war has continued]. Bombing each other, destroying everything ... for what? For f---ing what? People die, families are destroyed, children are traumatized and grow up with psychological problems ..."

On this Wednesday night, even as Shakhtar emerge as 3-1 victors over AEK, you're reminded once again of the difficulties. The team were up at 6 a.m. on Thursday to catch a 10 o'clock flight on a plane they chartered from a budget airline taking them back to Rzeszow in Poland. They'll then board a bus back across the border into Ukraine, arriving -- best-case scenario -- at 9 p.m. local time. All this not knowing whether they'll have power and heat when they arrive, or whether they'll be making regular trips into the air raid shelter.

You want to end on a note of hope. Srna does his best to offer it, but he clearly isn't going to lie to you or to himself.

"We [Croatians] have more or less an OK relationship now with Serbia," he says. "Time [30 years have passed] is helping, generations change, it's different people. We take a step back and understand what was good, what was not good. We can't say all Serbian people are bad ... But in this moment, it's not possible to be friends with a Russian person. In time, maybe a few years, maybe many years, I don't know ... right now though, it's impossible."

Certainly more impossible than a club without a home in a country at war defying logic and competing in the Champions League against the likes of Real Madrid, who visit Stamford Bridge on Jan. 27.

One of the side effects of war is the normalization of the horrific and the absurd. Shakhtar's plight has, by necessity, normalized the absurd, in an effort to stave off the horrific.

stories.headline: UFC champ Alexander Volkanovski proposes 'send-off' superbout vs. Justin Gaethje
stories.summary: UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski is calling for a "send-off" superfight against lightweight champion Justin Gaethje.
stories.body:
UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski has proposed a "send-off" superfight between himself and lightweight champion Justin Gaethje.

Volkanovski (28-4) is scheduled to defend his 145-pound title against Movsar Evloev (20-0) at UFC 333 on Oct. 24 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. Arguably the greatest featherweight of all time, Volkanovski has acknowledged he is approaching the end of his career at 38 years old. Gaethje, 37, has acknowledged the same since he claimed the UFC's 155-pound title for the first time in June.

With both champions seemingly near the end of their time in the Octagon, Volkanovski has suggested a winner-take-all scenario in 2027.

"Imagine that, do it as a send-off," Volkanovski told the "Who Da Fook Are These Guys?" podcast. "Gaethje, Volk. I think he's said that he maybe has one more. That could be a superfight. Let's do a superfight with the lightweight title on the line. We can both see everyone off with a crazy superfight. That could be really good."

Volkanovski, of Australia, has already tried to capture the lightweight title. He famously challenged then-lightweight champion Islam Makhachev twice in a 10-month span in 2023. He suffered a razor-close decision loss to Makhachev in their first meeting in February then lost by first-round knockout in an October rematch that was scheduled on short notice.

Gaethje (28-5) has not even guaranteed whether he will fight again or retire off his historic win at the White House in June, but he has stated that he believes his next challenger would be lightweight contender Arman Tsarukyan. Volkanovski appears to be throwing his name into the mix in the hope of changing those plans.

"He's said, 'What's the point of doing rematches,'" Volkanovski said. "Let's do a superfight then [retire] straight away after, let the divisions sort themselves out. The UFC would be happy for that. Let's make it happen."

stories.headline: Judge sides with NRL over NZ Rugby on Chiefs name
stories.summary: Rugby league has struck the first blow in the Chief name wars, with New Zealand Rugby's urgent injunction denied ahead of the new PNG NRL club's jersey reveal.
stories.body:
New Zealand's High Court has knocked back an application for an interim injunction on the PNG Chiefs NRL franchise using its name in the country.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) had rushed to court ahead of the PNG team's logo and jersey reveal in Port Moresby next week.

The organisation claimed use of the Chiefs name, also the name of the long-standing Super Rugby Pacific outfit, would cause confusion and damage to the brand value.

But a judge at Friday's two-hour Wellington hearing turned down the application after hearing an injunction could harm the NRL expansion outfit's efforts to attract players ahead of a 2028 debut.

The dispute remains though, with the application for a final injunction still before the court and legal action in Australia a consideration.

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys last week labelled NZR's action one of "mind-blowing hypocrisy", using the example of the Auckland Blues' arrival decades after the NSW Blues "had been the Blues".

"Today's decision is not a judgement on the strength of our case, and the matter will still be heard in full," NZR boss Steve Lancaster said.

"As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn't changed. We remain open to working with the ARLC on a solution."

NZR's lawyer Earl Gray argued on Friday that the PNG Chiefs' use of 'PNG Chiefs' and 'Chiefs' interchangeably created confusion for fans of both codes and that, with no clear distinction between the two, it would strip the rugby Chiefs' brand exclusivity.

He said NZR had trademark protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand that the NRL had not acknowledged.

ARLC laywer Clive Elliot argued that the request for an urgent injunction, about a year after NZR became aware of the PNG Chiefs name, was not appropriate.

He said an injunction now would cloud the franchise's reputation ahead of a recruitment blitz once free agency opens in November.

stories.headline: Premier League Top 50: Ranking the best players so far this season
stories.summary: The Premier League Top 50 returns for the 2026-27 season to rank the best players across the league so far.
stories.body:
Let's dig into the big question that's on everybody's mind: Who, uh, is the best player in the Premier League?

While we wait for the league to issue its punishment to Manchester City for breaking 114 rules and cheating their way to a spend of $1 billion more than regulations allowed, the games still go on.

Did you know Jordan Henderson scored twice last week? For Chelsea? Also: None of the promoted teams are in the relegation zone! Hull City are tied for seventh! Everton ... are tied for fourth?

To take stock of what has suddenly become -- and will continue to be -- the weirdest Premier League season of all time, we've decided to roll out the second edition of ESPN's Premier League Top 50, with our first coming before the season began.

We'll ask it again: Who is the best player in the Premier League? And now we'll answer it.

How we rank the players and who missed out

As we've done for the past two years, the rankings are meant to be a combination of true talent, how much value a player has actually provided and how much better that player is than the average players at his position.

The list is still tilted toward goal-producing-and-creating players on the best teams in England, but it opens up space for defenders and midfielders and goalkeepers from a bunch of different places up and down the table.

Injured players are ineligible, so you won't see the likes of Arsenal's William Saliba, Liverpool's Hugo Ekitike or Bournemouth's Alex Scott on the list.

You also won't see Liverpool's Bradley Barcola, who I'd expect to be on the list by the end of the season, but who has had almost no impact on any of the Premier League matches he has played thus far. A couple of other new signings -- Barcola's club and country teammate Jérémy Jacquet and Aston Villa's record signing Johan Manzambi -- have already broken into the top 50 with impressive starts to their Premier League careers.

Unless otherwise noted, most of the data you'll see throughout the piece comes from the stats app Futi. OK, let's get to the top 50...

50. Thierno Barry, striker, Everton

There's a great new book by David Epstein called "Inside the Box." It's, essentially, about how we tend to be at our best -- whether on our own or as groups -- where we're forced into constraints.

There are infinitely more options at our disposal today compared with 30 years ago; constraints help with that problem. But they also seem to make us more creative, more productive and happier.

See: Everton Football Club. Last summer they signed a promising young striker from Villarreal with a nice track record of getting lots of high-quality shots. But he was mostly a backup behind the veteran Beto, who left this offseason.

Everton tried to sign U.S. men's national team standout Folarin Balogun on the final day of the transfer window -- only for it to fall apart because of issues Everton had with Balogun's medical clearance exam.

So, without any other options, David Moyes was forced to play Thierno Barry. Through six matches, he has scored three times and ranks second in non-penalty expected goals.

49. Anton Stach, central midfielder, Leeds United

48. Sávio, winger, Tottenham Hotspur

47. Florian Wirtz, attacking midfielder, Liverpool

What if I told you there was a player who was second on Liverpool in expected goals, third in expected assists, second in passes into the penalty area, first in through balls, first in progressive passes received, first in carries into the penalty area and first in balls won by pressing high?

You might not be screaming "$150-MILLION PLAYER" -- but you also probably wouldn't be spending every weekend talking about how he's not good enough to play for Liverpool. And yet, that's pretty much where the discussion lands every time Florian Wirtz plays a game.

Wirtz still hasn't produced enough in front of goal to match the record fee Liverpool paid to acquire him, but there's a long way between that and not being good enough to play.

The promise of Wirtz was someone who did all the little things that helped you win and gave you 20 goals+assists at the same time. The latter hasn't been there; the former still has. Per Futi's possession-value ratings, he has been Liverpool's fourth-most valuable player this season.

46. Johan Manzambi, attacking midfielder, Aston Villa

45. Matheus Cunha, forward, Manchester United

44. Kai Havertz, striker, Arsenal

43. Morgan Rogers, attacking midfielder, Chelsea

42. Jérémy Jacquet, center back, Liverpool

41. Daniel Muñoz, right back, Nottingham Forest

40. Pedro Neto, winger, Chelsea

39. Ryan Gravenberch, defensive midfielder, Liverpool

38. Diogo Dalot, right back, Manchester United

37. Matheus Nunes, right back, Manchester City

Both Diogo Dalot and Matheus Nunes are simply very good fullbacks -- somewhat improbably.

Dalot, unlike his countryman and city-mate, has always been a fullback, and he's one of the few ever-presents for Manchester United over the past half-decade of volatility at the club. He might be the least spectacular player in the league, which I think makes him interesting to talk about.

When a player doesn't have a standout skill, it's usually used as a reason for why he won't hack it at the top level. Dalot has never really had a standout skill, but all his skills slowly improved and now he's above-average at everything. He's the same exact kind of player he always was -- just better in every way.

Nunes is the opposite: Coaches loved him for what they thought they could mold his athleticism into, but he just wasn't good enough on the ball in tight spaces to do anything consistently in the midfield, first for Wolves then for Man City. Then Pep Guardiola moved him to fullback, and after a year or so of growing pains, he's one of the best right backs in the league.

Two totally different players, arriving at the same point, right around the same time.

36. Bart Verbruggen, goalkeeper, Brighton

35. Emiliano Martínez, goalkeeper, Chelsea

34. David Raya, goalkeeper, Arsenal

These above players were my top three goalkeepers coming into the season, and nothing has changed my opinion on that.

Per Gradient Sports, they're three of the only four keepers who have received a positive shot-stopping grade on at least 30% of the shots they've faced. On top of that, none one of them have received a single negative shot-stopping grade, which essentially means that none have made a mistake when facing a shot.

Past research from Gradient found that avoiding shot-stopping mistakes is the most repeatable goalkeeper skill. What makes great keepers great for more than a single season, in other words, is their ability to consistently save the savable shots rather than their ability to tip away the ball that's bound for the upper corner.

Raya, in particular, stands out in this way. While he doesn't have any seasons where he has conceded 10 goals fewer than an expected-goals model might suggest -- something we've seen from the likes of Jan Oblak, Thibaut Courtois, David de Gea, and Alisson Becker over the past generation -- he has made just six shot-stopping errors, per Gradient, over the past three seasons combined.

33. Lisandro Martínez, center back, Manchester United

32. Ezri Konsa, center back, Arsenal

31. Adam Wharton, central midfielder, Crystal Palace

30. Cody Gakpo, winger, Liverpool

29. Youri Tielemans, central midfielder, Manchester United

28. Alexander Isak, striker, Liverpool

27. Pascal Gross, central midfielder, Brighton

Here's a chart comparing everyone that Futi classifies as a midfielder across the two main attacking statistics: expected goals and expected assists.

You'll notice three players in the upper right: Arsenal captain Martin Ødegaard, former Premier League Player of the Year Phil Foden and ... 35-year-old Pascal Gross. That's shocking enough on its face...

But then just take a look at where he's actually touching the ball:

Most of Gross's touches are coming in the middle third or the right half-space -- the Kevin De Bruyne zone -- just on the edge of the attacking third. Only Brighton's center backs, Lewis Dunk and Luka Vuskovic, have attempted more passes than Gross this season.

Gross is not a low-touch midfielder who only needs to contribute around the penalty area. No, he's a high-touch midfielder who is also contributing around the penalty area -- in the toughest league in the world, for the team currently in third place, at 35 years old!

He's one of the most underrated players in Premier League history: a truly elite passer who has done it for a decade straight.

26. Phil Foden, attacking midfielder, Manchester City

It was all going so well for Foden, too.

After literally winning the Premier League Player of the Season award in 2023-24, Foden quickly fell out of favor with manager Pep Guardiola. It's not like he never played, but he was never a clear first-choice option over the past two seasons.

After starting for England at Euro 2024, he didn't even make the roster for this past summer's World Cup despite being fully healthy.

But this season, he started four of City's first five matches in the league and in the Champions League, and he looked much closer to the guy we saw three seasons ago. Then he kicked Bruno Fernandes, got a straight red card and was suspended for City's final match before the international break during which City were found guilty of 114 different cheating charges.

Even if Foden comes back into the lineup -- and he should because he has been way more productive than Antoine Semenyo or Iliman Ndiaye -- and picks up where he left off, then what will it really mean?

With what's expected to be a severe punishment looming in the background, City's matches currently exist in a netherworld where they seem to mean everything and nothing at the same time. Each City match is going to be the most important match every weekend -- the team the league says cheated, still playing in that league -- but we all expect there to be some kind of punishment that likely renders those results moot.

And after that punishment happens, the games could enter into an even stranger realm of un-meaning: where City win most of their games and still finish in last, or where City stop trying in the Premier League and focus all their efforts on Europe.

But, uh, yeah: Phil Foden seemed like he was back, for a couple of games.

25. Cole Palmer, attacking midfielder, Chelsea

24. João Pedro, striker, Chelsea

23. Jan Paul van Hecke, center back, Tottenham Hotspur

22. Jurriën Timber, right back, Arsenal

21. Nico O'Reilly, left back, Manchester City

20. Reece James, right back, Chelsea

19. Enzo Fernández, central midfielder, Manchester City

18. Josko Gvardiol, center back, Manchester City

17. Bruno Guimarães, central midfielder, Arsenal

16. Riccardo Calafiori, left back, Arsenal

This statement is true: manager Mikel Arteta has relied quite heavily on players who used to be center backs to play fullback for his team.

This statement is also true: That has mostly been a conservative decision, one that has helped Arsenal become the best defensive team in the world but also one that has hamstrung the team's attacking proficiency in open play and required them to become the greatest set piece team we've ever seen.

Another true statement: The majority of Calafiori's minutes before joining Arsenal -- both with Italy and with Bologna -- were played as a center back on the left side of a back three.

And now a false statement: Calafiori is just like all the other defense-first center backs Arteta converted to fullback.

Calafiori is a better defender than your average fullback, especially in the air, but "conservative" is one of the last words I'd use to describe him. Check out where he's touching the ball this season:

Let's just follow it from left to right: starts off pretty normal. In his own half, he's staying wide like most fullbacks do, providing a wide passing option and opening up space between the lines for a midfielder to receive a pass. That remains mostly true in the middle third; he gets a little zanier and comes in field to create rotations that help Arsenal break into the attacking third, but he's still mostly out wide.

Once he's in the attacking third, though? Pretty much anything can happen -- other than what you'd expect. See how there's barely anything along the sideline once you cross past the top of the box? The one thing Calafiori doesn't do is the one thing every other attacking fullback has always done: overlap his winger.

Based on where a player actually touches a ball and what he does with it, Futi's data classifies players into a spectrum of roles. Some 53% of the time it sees Calafiori as a wide defender; 13% of the time he's a central attacker (basically a No. 10); 16% of the time he's a wide attacker; and 18% of the time? The model thinks he's playing as a forward.

15. Rúben Dias, center back, Manchester City

14. Virgil van Dijk, center back, Liverpool

13. Dominik Szoboszlai, central midfielder, Liverpool

12. Elliot Anderson, central midfielder, Manchester City

11. Bryan Mbeumo, winger, Manchester United

He's not a superstar, and maybe he shouldn't be this high. But at a time when it seems like most of the truly devastating attacking players are currently playing outside of England, it feels especially valuable to have a player who is going to give you something reliable.

Really, Mbeumo might be the most consistent attacker in the league. Over the past four seasons, he's averaging the following, in order, for non-penalty goals+assists per 90 minutes: 0.50, 0.55, 0.58, 0.48. That averages out to around 0.51 goals+assists per 90 minutes. This season? He's at 0.5.

Throw in a little bit of everything else -- passing, carrying, off-ball running, defensive effort -- and his impact is even a little more valuable than what those numbers suggest.

10. Martin Ødegaard, attacking midfielder, Arsenal

9. Moisés Caicedo, defensive midfielder, Chelsea

8. Marc Guéhi, center back, Manchester City

After some hiccups once he joined Man City midway through last season, he has been the best center back in the league so far this season. He even spent significant minutes as a midfielder and played quite well.

Perhaps the biggest compliment I can give him is that although he's only 6-foot tall -- quite small for a center back -- you never really notice it when you watch him play.

7. Jérémy Doku, winger, Manchester City

6. Gabriel Magalhães, center back, Arsenal

5. Bruno Fernandes, attacking midfielder, Manchester United

4. Rayan Cherki, attacking midfielder, Manchester City

3. Bukayo Saka, winger, Arsenal

2. Declan Rice, central midfielder, Arsenal

1. Erling Haaland, striker, Manchester City

We're just six games into the season, and I feel comfortable making a conclusion: There's a clear top tier of players in the Premier League, and it consists of the four guys at the top of these rankings.

Cherki is playing a starter's load finally, and that has led to is him leading the league in expected assists. Oh, and he's ninth in non-penalty expected goals. There's not a single player in Europe that I'd rather have on the ball against a packed-in defense.

As you can see above, Bukayo Saka might be making a leap in front of goal, and he's still one of the best dribblers in the league and probably the best defender in Europe among the guys who can consider themselves elite attackers.

Rice, meanwhile, continues to be excellent at every aspect of the sport, in every area of the field, in any phase of the game. I'm running out of things to say about him, so I just say the same thing every single time.

... As I do with Haaland: There's nothing new here. He's involved in 3% of Man City's phases of play -- near the bottom of the league. And yet he leads the league in goals. He has 118 in 133 Premier League starts.

How many more will he get? All of a sudden, that's a question with a bunch of different answers.

stories.headline: Halpin’s go-ahead homer flips Game 3 as Guardians beat Rays 3-2 for 2-1 AL Championship Series lead
stories.summary: — In a season where Cleveland rookies helped propel to the Guardians to their third straight AL Central title, it was the team's emotional spark plug that powered the Guardians to a pivotal victory in Game 3 of the AL Championship Series.
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- — In a season where Cleveland rookies helped propel to the Guardians to their third straight AL Central title, it was the team's emotional spark plug that powered the Guardians to a pivotal victory in Game 3 of the AL Championship Series.


Petey Halpin hit a go-ahead, two-run homer in the fifth inning and followed with a majestic bat flip as the Guardians beat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 Thursday for a 2-1 lead in the best-of-seven series.


“It’s the second time he’s kind of picked us up in a big spot this year. And a really fun moment for him, great swing,” Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said.


Halpin watched the ball clear the wall in right-center and then launched his bat over his head and into the sky before rounding the bases. The bat might have gone higher than the 25-degree launch angle on his homer.


“I definitely threw it high. I think just the moment and that being for sure the biggest moment of my career, just the energy and the excitement, just kind of let it go,” Halpin said.


The home run and the bat flip energized Cleveland's dugout and the 30,101 fans in attendance at Progressive Field. Even though the game wasn't sold out, it was a strong crowd after the start time was moved up five hours on Wednesday due to the threat of rain.


“That was a nasty one. Didn’t even move either. I feel like he knew that the wind was blowing in and it still got out," outfielder Steven Kwan said. "So the bat flip that he did was just ignorant, but in a good way. That was awesome.”


Gavin Williams struck out nine over five innings. José Ramírez had two hits and Nathaniel Lowe added an RBI double in the second inning for the Guardians, who have won five of their last six playoff games since trailing the Chicago White Sox 2-0 in their AL Division Series.


“When anyone does their job and gets the job done and puts on us in a position to win, everyone on the team’s juiced. It’s not about me or that home run, but it’s just the fact that we’re winning and we keep rolling,” Halpin said.


Chandler Simpson had a two-run triple in the fourth inning for Tampa Bay, which was held to three hits and struck out 13 times.


Game 4 is scheduled for Friday, though rain is forecast.


Bailey's infield single sets stage for Halpin
Patrick Bailey started the fifth with a chop that Rays starting pitcher Griffin Jax was unable to cleanly field. Five pitches later, Halpin connected on a elevated 95.9 mph sinker on a 2-2 count and drove it 385 feet into the stands in right-center for a 3-2 lead.


It was Halpin’s first postseason home run and only the fifth overall of his two year big league career. It was the first time Jax allowed a homer since Sept. 9, a span of five appearances.


“I knew I hit it good. I thought I got more of it, I guess,” Halpin said. “I knew that he used a sinker in a few times to lefties before, kind of as a strikeout pitch. I was on a hard timing trying to get the head out and it all worked out. He left it over the plate a little bit and I was able to make a good swing.”


Rays manager Kevin Cash said Jax wouldn't have been able to make a play on Bailey's chop, especially with the jump Bailey got leaving the batter's box. The sinker to Halpin leaked over the plate.


“He does a good job handling off-speed, so it was the right pitch. Just the wrong location," Jax said.


Halpin flourishes in lineup
Halpin got his first postseason start in Game 5 of the ALDS and had two doubles. He is 4 for 11 with a home run and two RBI in the past four games.


The 24-year old outfielder also had a three-run homer on Sept. 16 against the White Sox, which put the Guardians atop the AL Central.


“He’s ready for whatever we ask him to do. He got called up when everybody got hurt, and he played an everyday role for us for a while. And then it kind of turned into a defensive replacement. And then kind of filling in for injured guys,” Vogt said. “I don’t feel like any moment ever gets too big for him. And so it’s really fun when you see somebody like that step up for their teammates.”


Another strong start for Williams
Williams allowed two runs in five innings with one walk. He is 2-0 with a 2.16 ERA and 33 strikeouts over 16 2/3 innings in four postseason games this season, including three starts.


Cleveland retired 16 of the Rays' last 17 batters. Daniel Espino, Erik Sabrowski, Hunter Gaddis and Cade Smith allowed only one baserunner the final four innings.


Smith stranded a runner at third in the eighth when he struck out Yandy Díaz in a 10-pitch at-bat, then retired the Rays in order in the ninth.


Rays offense held in check
Other than Simpson's triple, it was another quiet day for the Rays' offense Williams didn’t allow a baserunner and struck out five his time through the order.


Tampa Bay batters were retired in order in seven innings, and Junior Caminero had four strikeouts. Rays batters whiffed 13 times after combining for 14 in the first two games.


It is the first time the Rays trailed 2-1 in three ALCS appearances.


“Two runs on two hits. You got to be perfect to win games like that,” Cash said.
